title: Increased phototoxic burn tolerance time and quality of life in patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria treated with afamelanotide – a three years observational study

citation.title: Increased phototoxic burn tolerance time and quality of life in patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria treated with afamelanotide – a three years observational study

printed_heading.text: RESEARCH Open Access Increased phototoxic burn tolerance time and quality of life in patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria treated with afamelanotide – a three years observational study Jasmin Barman-Aksözen1 , Michèle Nydegger2 , Xiaoye Schneider-Yin1 and Anna-Elisabeth Minder3*

what_it_measured.text: We investigated whether the time span since the preceding implant influenced the PBTT in our cohort.
As this study relies on retrospectively collected information, we first determined whether the data results in meaningful observations (for full information see supplement 1).

dose.text: Afamelanotide is administered subcutaneously as a 16 mg slow release implant formulation with a therapeutic effect of approximately 60 days [21, 25].

route.text: Afamelanotide is administered subcutaneously as a 16 mg slow release implant formulation with a therapeutic effect of approximately 60 days [21, 25].

endpoint.text: Methods: We analysed clinical data collected between 2016 and 2018 in the Swiss EPP cohort (n = 39) on maximum phototoxic burn tolerance time (PBTT), i.e., maximum time spent in sunlight without phototoxic reaction, severity of phototoxic reactions as assessed by an 11-point Likert-type visual analogue scale (VAS), with 0 being no pain and 10 being the worst possible pain, and Quality of Life (QoL), as assessed with an EPP-specific instrument.

reported_results.text: Individual PBPF increased 1.8- to 180-fold (full range, median 15).
The extent of the increased PBTT under treatment was independent of the reported PBTT before treatment (Kendall’s tau = 0.105, n = 37; p = 0.41).
In our cohort, all patients under treatment increased their individual PBTT and afamelanotide provided a median PBPF of 15 (IQR 6–36, range 1.8–180, n = 37; p < 0.0001).
Under treatment with afamelanotide, the PBTT significantly increased to a median of 180 min (IQR 120–240 min, range 15–420 min, n = 37 (2 patients with missing data); p < 0.0001) (see Fig. 1).
The QoL in continuously treated patients remained unchanged throughout the observation period (median QoL 66.7– 83.3%, p = 0.24).
At baseline, i.e. the QoL before the first treatment, they showed a median QoL of 49.1% (IQR 16.4–65.5).
